ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: A small lunar lander is connected to the space station, and together they make circular motion around the Moon. Its orbital radius is 3 times the radius of the Moon. At a certain moment, the space station makes the lunar lander decelerate and separate. The lunar lander lands on the Moon along the elliptical orbit shown in the figure. After staying on the lunar surface for a period of time to complete scientific investigation work, it quickly starts and still returns along the original elliptical orbit. When it first returns to the separation point, it just docks with the space station. The rapid start time of the lunar lander can be ignored. During the whole process, the space station keeps running around the Moon in the original orbit. It is known that the gravitational acceleration on the lunar surface is g, and the radius of the Moon is R. Ignoring the influence of the Moon's rotation, the shortest time that the lunar lander can stay on the Moon is approximately (　　)

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: the gray circle in the figure represents the Moon, and outside it there is a large circular orbit centered on the Moon. At the top there is a rectangle representing the space station or the separation point; starting from this top point there is also an elliptical orbit. The apolune end of the ellipse is at the top and is tangent to the outer circular orbit, and the perilune end is tangent to the lunar surface. The arrows indicate the direction in which the lunar lander descends and returns along the ellipse. Therefore, combined with the problem statement, the separation point is on the circular orbit with radius 3R and is the apolune point of the transfer ellipse; when landing on the Moon, it contacts the lunar surface and is the perilune point of the transfer ellipse. Then reason: the apolune radius of the transfer ellipse is r_a=3R, and the perilune radius is r_p=R, so the semi-major axis a=(r_a+r_p)/2=(3R+R)/2=2R. The gravitational acceleration on the lunar surface satisfies g=μ/R^2, therefore the lunar gravitational parameter μ=gR^2. The space station always moves on the circular orbit with radius 3R, and its period is T_s=2π√((3R)^3/μ)=2π√(27R^3/(gR^2))=6√3π√(R/g). The lunar lander uses half an elliptical period to descend from the separation point along the ellipse to the lunar surface, and after rapid start it uses another half an elliptical period to return from the lunar surface to the separation point along the same ellipse. Therefore the pure flight time is equal to one complete period of this ellipse: T_e=2π√(a^3/μ)=2π√((2R)^3/(gR^2))=4√2π√(R/g). In order to dock with the space station when it first returns to the separation point, the total elapsed time T_e+τ of the lunar lander must equal an integer multiple of the space station's period: T_e+τ=nT_s. Also because T_e<T_s, the shortest nonnegative stay time takes n=1, τ=T_s-T_e=(6√3-4√2)π√(R/g). Numerically, 6√3-4√2≈4.7. Final answer: the shortest time that the lunar lander can stay on the Moon is approximately 4.7π√(R/g).
